CHAPTER 1.3 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.3 · LEARNING AREA 1 · OCTOBER

Rules of differentiation

Working out every derivative from the limit of the difference quotient would be laborious. A few rules are enough to differentiate almost any function: powers, sums, products and compositions, plus $e^x$, $\ln x$ and $\sin x$. In the advanced course you prove rules instead of just using them, and you learn the way back: finding the function that belongs to a derivative.

15 LESSONS3 UNITS3 PRACTICE PAGESPROOFS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • apply the power, constant multiple and sum rules, also for rational exponents, and prove a rule
  • differentiate $e^x$, $\ln x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ without aids
  • differentiate combinations and compositions with the product rule and the chain rule
  • reverse differentiation for power functions: find a function $F$ with $F' = f$ for a given $f$

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1Powers, sums and the reversal

Written as powers: $(x^2)' = 2x^1$, $(x^3)' = 3x^2$, $(x^{-1})' = -1 \cdot x^{-2}$. The exponent moves to the front as a factor, the new exponent is 1 smaller. For $x^{10}$ this predicts $10x^9$, for $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ the value $\tfrac12 x^{-1/2} = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$, exactly the result from chapter 1.2.

KEY POINT · POWER, CONSTANT MULTIPLE AND SUM RULES

Power rule: $\left(x^r\right)' = r \cdot x^{r - 1}$ for every rational number $r$ (for $x > 0$ if $x^r$ is not defined otherwise).

Constant multiple rule: $(c \cdot f)' = c \cdot f'$ · sum rule: $(f + g)' = f' + g'$. Constants drop out when differentiating.

Reversal: a function $F$ with $F' = f$ is called an antiderivative of $f$. For $f(x) = x^n$ ($n \neq -1$) it is $F(x) = \tfrac{1}{n + 1} x^{n + 1} + C$ with any constant $C$.

Proof of the sum rule: $\tfrac{(f + g)(x + h) - (f + g)(x)}{h} = \tfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} + \tfrac{g(x + h) - g(x)}{h}$, and by the limit theorem for sums this tends to $f'(x) + g'(x)$.

Check: you always check an antiderivative by differentiating.

INTERACTIVE · DIFFERENTIATION TRAINER

New exercises at the touch of a button. Type in $f'(x)$; it is checked at many points.

EXAMPLE 1 · PROOF OF THE POWER RULE FOR n ∈ ℕ

Prove $\left(x^n\right)' = n x^{n - 1}$ for natural numbers $n$.

By the binomial theorem, $(x + h)^n = x^n + n x^{n - 1} h + h^2 \cdot R(x, h)$, where $R$ is a polynomial in $x$ and $h$.

So $\tfrac{(x + h)^n - x^n}{h} = n x^{n - 1} + h \cdot R(x, h) \to$ $n x^{n - 1}$ for $h \to 0$.

EXAMPLE 2 · DIFFERENTIATING AND REVERSING

a) Differentiate $f(x) = 4x^3 - 2\sqrt{x} + \tfrac{5}{x}$.   b) Give all $F$ with $F'(x) = 3x^2 + 4x$ and the one with $F(1) = 5$.

a) $f'(x) = 12x^2 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - \tfrac{5}{x^2}$

b) $F(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + C$. $F(1) = 3 + C = 5$: $F(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + 2$

INTERACTIVE · ANTIDERIVATIVES

At the top the antiderivatives $F + C$, at the bottom $f$. The gradient of $F$ at the dragged point is exactly the function value of $f$.

EXERCISES

Differentiate: a) $x^5$   b) $3x^{-2}$   c) $\sqrt[3]{x}$   d) $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$   e) $\pi^2$

a) $5x^4$   b) $-6x^{-3}$   c) $\tfrac13 x^{-2/3}$   d) $2 \cdot \left(-\tfrac12\right) x^{-3/2} = -x^{-3/2}$   e) 0, a constant

Differentiate: a) $f(x) = 2x^4 - 3x^2 + 7x - 1$   b) $g(t) = \tfrac12 t^2 + \tfrac{1}{t}$

a) $8x^3 - 6x + 7$   b) $t - \tfrac{1}{t^2}$

Give an antiderivative and check it: a) $f(x) = x^4 - 6x$   b) $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x^2}$   c) $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$

a) $\tfrac15 x^5 - 3x^2$   b) $-\tfrac1x$   c) $\tfrac23 x^{3/2}$ (each $+ C$)

Prove the constant multiple rule $(c \cdot f)' = c \cdot f'$ with the difference quotient.

$\tfrac{c f(x + h) - c f(x)}{h} = c \cdot \tfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \to c \cdot f'(x)$, because by the limit theorem for products you may take constant factors out of the limit.

A body moves according to $s(t) = 2t^3 - 3t^2$ (metres, seconds). Find the velocity $v = s'$ and the acceleration $a = v'$. When does it stand still for a moment? How fast is it after 2 s?

$v(t) = 6t^2 - 6t$, $a(t) = 12t - 6$. Standstill at $t = 0$ and $t = 1$ s. $v(2) = 12$ m/s, $a(2) = 18$ m/s².

$12 - 1 - 5 = 6$

Calculate the derivative of $\sqrt{x}$ at the point 4.

$\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt4} = \tfrac14$

$F'(x) = 2x$ and $F(0) = 3$. Calculate $F(2)$.

$F(x) = x^2 + 3$, $F(2) = 7$

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2eˣ, ln x, sin x and the product rule

For $x \cdot x^2$, “derivative times derivative” gives the term $1 \cdot 2x = 2x$, but $3x^2$ is correct. For the rectangle the area grows by two strips, $u \cdot \Delta v$ and $v \cdot \Delta u$, and a tiny corner. The corner disappears in the limit, the strips give $u v' + u' v$: for $x \cdot x^2$ exactly $x \cdot 2x + 1 \cdot x^2 = 3x^2$.

KEY POINT · SPECIAL FUNCTIONS AND THE PRODUCT RULE

$\left(e^x\right)' = e^x$ · $\left(a^x\right)' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ · $(\ln x)' = \tfrac{1}{x}$ for $x > 0$ · $(\sin x)' = \cos x$ · $(\cos x)' = -\sin x$

Product rule: $(u \cdot v)' = u' \cdot v + u \cdot v'$

Proof: $\tfrac{u(x + h)v(x + h) - u(x)v(x)}{h} = \tfrac{u(x + h) - u(x)}{h} \cdot v(x + h) + u(x) \cdot \tfrac{v(x + h) - v(x)}{h}$. Because $v$ is continuous, $v(x + h) \to v(x)$, and the expression tends to $u'v + uv'$.

Why $(\ln x)' = \tfrac1x$? $\ln$ is the inverse function of $e^x$. At the point $(\ln a, a)$, $e^x$ has the gradient $a$; reflected in $y = x$, this becomes the gradient $\tfrac1a$ at the point $(a, \ln a)$.

Without aids, according to the curriculum, you must master all the derivatives of this unit. You do not need the quotient rule without aids.

INTERACTIVE · THE PRODUCT RULE AS A RECTANGLE

Make $h$ smaller. The red corner $\Delta u \cdot \Delta v$ shrinks much faster than the two strips.

EXAMPLE 3 · PRODUCT WITH eˣ

Differentiate $f(x) = x^2 e^x$.

$u = x^2$, $v = e^x$: $f'(x) = 2x \cdot e^x + x^2 \cdot e^x$.

$f'(x) = (x^2 + 2x)\,e^x$. Factorising pays off: $f'(x) = 0 \iff x = 0$ or $x = -2$, because $e^x$ is never 0.

EXAMPLE 4 · PRODUCT WITH ln x

Differentiate $g(x) = x \ln x$ and find where the graph has a horizontal tangent.

$g'(x) = 1 \cdot \ln x + x \cdot \tfrac1x = \ln x + 1$.

$\ln x + 1 = 0 \iff x = e^{-1}$: horizontal tangent at $x = \tfrac1e \approx 0.368$.

INTERACTIVE · TANGENT AND NORMAL

Choose a function and drag the point: tangent and normal with their equations.

EXERCISES

Differentiate: a) $3e^x - 2\sin x$   b) $5\ln x + \cos x$   c) $2^x + x^2$   d) $e^2 + \ln 3$

a) $3e^x - 2\cos x$   b) $\tfrac{5}{x} - \sin x$   c) $\ln 2 \cdot 2^x + 2x$   d) 0, only constants

Differentiate with the product rule: a) $x^3 \sin x$   b) $e^x \cos x$   c) $\sqrt{x}\,\ln x$

a) $3x^2 \sin x + x^3 \cos x$   b) $e^x(\cos x - \sin x)$   c) $\tfrac{\ln x}{2\sqrt{x}} + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$

Find the tangents a) to $\ln x$ at the point $(1, 0)$   b) to $\sin x$ at the origin   c) to $e^x$ at the point $(0, 1)$.

a) $y = x - 1$   b) $y = x$   c) $y = x + 1$. All three are tangents with gradient 1.

Justify $(\ln x)' = \tfrac1x$ in detail with the inverse function: which points correspond, which gradients?

The point $(a, \ln a)$ on $\ln$ corresponds to the mirror point $(\ln a, a)$ on $e^x$. There the gradient is $e^{\ln a} = a$. Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$, so the gradient becomes its reciprocal: $\tfrac1a$.

$f(x) = x e^x$. Find $f'$, $f''$ and $f'''$. Conjecture a formula for the $n$-th derivative and justify it with the product rule (induction from $n$ to $n + 1$).

$f' = (x + 1)e^x$, $f'' = (x + 2)e^x$, $f''' = (x + 3)e^x$. Conjecture $f^{(n)}(x) = (x + n)e^x$. If it holds for $n$, then $f^{(n+1)} = 1 \cdot e^x + (x + n)e^x = (x + n + 1)e^x$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$f(x) = x^2 e^x$. Calculate $f'(0)$.

$(0 + 0)\,e^0 = 0$

$g(x) = x \ln x$. Calculate $g'(e)$.

$\ln e + 1 = 2$

What is $(\cos x)'$?

At $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the cosine falls with gradient −1.

UNIT 35 LESSONS

3The chain rule

$(3x + 1)^2 = 9x^2 + 6x + 1$ has the derivative $18x + 6 = 2(3x + 1) \cdot 3$. The outer function “square” gives $2(3x + 1)$, and because the inside $3x + 1$ grows three times as fast as $x$, the factor 3 is added. For $(3x + 1)^{20}$ you get $20(3x + 1)^{19} \cdot 3$ without any calculation.

KEY POINT · CHAIN RULE

If $f(x) = u(v(x))$ with an inner function $v$ differentiable at $x$ and an outer function $u$ differentiable at $v(x)$, then $$f'(x) = u'(v(x)) \cdot v'(x)$$ “outer derivative times inner derivative”.

Linear composition: $\left(g(ax + b)\right)' = a \cdot g'(ax + b)$, for example $\left(e^{2x - 5}\right)' = 2e^{2x - 5}$ and $\left(\ln(3x - 5)\right)' = \tfrac{3}{3x - 5}$.

For products of compositions use the product rule first, and inside it the chain rule for each factor.

In Leibniz’s notation the rule looks like calculating with fractions: $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = \tfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}v} \cdot \tfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}$. That is not a proof, but it is a good memory aid.

Common mistake: forgetting the inner derivative. $\left(\sin(2x)\right)' = 2\cos(2x)$, not $\cos(2x)$.

INTERACTIVE · OUTER TIMES INNER DERIVATIVE

Choose an outer and an inner function. The tangent at the dragged point has exactly the gradient $u'(v(x)) \cdot v'(x)$.

EXAMPLE 5 · THREE EXAMPLES FROM THE CURRICULUM

Differentiate: a) $f(x) = 3x^2 e^{2x - 5}$   b) $g(x) = \ln(3x - 5)$   c) $k(x) = \tfrac12 x^2 \sin(2x - 1)$

a) $6x\,e^{2x - 5} + 3x^2 \cdot 2e^{2x - 5} = 6x(1 + x)\,e^{2x - 5}$   b) $\tfrac{3}{3x - 5}$ for $x > \tfrac53$

c) $x \sin(2x - 1) + \tfrac12 x^2 \cdot 2\cos(2x - 1) = x\sin(2x - 1) + x^2 \cos(2x - 1)$

EXAMPLE 6 · aˣ ONCE MORE

Differentiate $a^x$ with the chain rule by writing $a = e^{\ln a}$.

$a^x = \left(e^{\ln a}\right)^x = e^{x \ln a}$, inner function $x \ln a$ with the derivative $\ln a$.

$\left(a^x\right)' = e^{x \ln a} \cdot \ln a = \ln a \cdot a^x$, the same as from the definition in chapter 1.2.

EXERCISES

Differentiate: a) $e^{3x}$   b) $\sin(2x + 1)$   c) $\sqrt{4x + 1}$   d) $(1 - x)^7$   e) $\ln(x^2 + 1)$

a) $3e^{3x}$   b) $2\cos(2x + 1)$   c) $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{4x + 1}}$   d) $-7(1 - x)^6$   e) $\tfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$

Differentiate: a) $(x^2 + 1)^5$   b) $e^{-x^2}$   c) $\cos(\pi x)$

a) $10x(x^2 + 1)^4$   b) $-2x\,e^{-x^2}$   c) $-\pi\sin(\pi x)$

Differentiate and simplify: a) $x^2 e^{-x}$   b) $x\sqrt{2x + 1}$   c) $e^{2x}\sin(3x)$

a) $(2x - x^2)e^{-x}$   b) $\sqrt{2x + 1} + \tfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x + 1}} = \tfrac{3x + 1}{\sqrt{2x + 1}}$   c) $e^{2x}\left(2\sin(3x) + 3\cos(3x)\right)$

Find the tangent to $f(x) = e^{-x^2}$ at the point $x = 1$.

$f(1) = e^{-1}$, $f'(x) = -2x e^{-x^2}$, $f'(1) = -2e^{-1}$. $t(x) = e^{-1} - 2e^{-1}(x - 1) = \tfrac{3 - 2x}{e} \approx 1.104 - 0.736x$.

Derive the quotient rule by writing $\tfrac{u}{v} = u \cdot v^{-1}$ and applying the product and chain rules. (The curriculum does not require it without aids; the derivation is a nice exercise.)

$\left(u \cdot v^{-1}\right)' = u' v^{-1} + u \cdot (-1)v^{-2} \cdot v' = \tfrac{u'}{v} - \tfrac{uv'}{v^2} = \tfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$

$f(x) = e^{3x}$. Calculate $f'(0)$.

$3e^0 = 3$

$g(x) = \ln(3x - 5)$. Calculate $g'(2)$.

$\tfrac{3}{6 - 5} = 3$

What is $\left(\sin(2x)\right)'$?

Do not forget the inner derivative 2.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Differentiate without aids: a) $\tfrac{x^3}{3} - 4\sqrt{x}$   b) $x\,e^{2x}$   c) $\ln(5x)$   d) $\sin^2 x$

a) $x^2 - \tfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$   b) $(1 + 2x)e^{2x}$   c) $\tfrac{5}{5x} = \tfrac1x$   d) $2\sin x \cos x$

Connecting with physics: a spring oscillates according to $s(t) = 2\sin(3t)$. Find $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ and show that $a(t) = -9\,s(t)$.

$v(t) = 6\cos(3t)$, $a(t) = -18\sin(3t) = -9 \cdot 2\sin(3t) = -9s(t)$. The acceleration points opposite to the displacement and is proportional to it: a harmonic oscillation.

Use $\ln(5x) = \ln 5 + \ln x$ to show that $\ln(5x)$ and $\ln x$ have the same derivative. What does that mean for the graphs?

$\ln 5$ is a constant, its derivative is 0. The graphs arise from each other by shifting up by $\ln 5$; at every point they have the same gradient.

Find all points in the interval $[0, 2\pi]$ at which $f(x) = e^{x}\sin x$ has a horizontal tangent.

$f'(x) = e^x(\sin x + \cos x) = 0 \iff \sin x = -\cos x \iff \tan x = -1$: $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $x = \tfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

How the number e got its name

Around 1685 Jakob Bernoulli asked a question about compound interest: a deposit earns 100 % interest a year. If it is credited every half year, the deposit grows to $1.5^2 = 2.25$, quarterly to $1.25^4 \approx 2.44$, monthly to $\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{12}\right)^{12} \approx 2.61$. How far do you get if interest is added more and more often? The answer is a limit, the number $2.718\,28\ldots$ (exercise 17 in Review · Deepen · Connect of chapter 1.1).

Leonhard Euler gave it the name $e$. He was already using the letter in 1727 or 1728 in a manuscript on cannon shots; it appeared in print for the first time in 1736 in his textbook on mechanics. Euler never revealed why he chose $e$ of all letters. That $e^x$, of all functions, is its own derivative makes the number the most important constant of analysis after $\pi$.

Source: Leonhard Euler: “Mechanica sive motus scientia analytice exposita”, volume 1, St Petersburg 1736 (the first printed use of the letter $e$ for the number).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

POWER, CONSTANT MULTIPLE, SUM

$(x^r)' = r x^{r - 1}$, $(cf)' = cf'$, $(f + g)' = f' + g'$

$\left(4x^3 - 2\sqrt{x}\right)' = 12x^2 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$

SPECIAL FUNCTIONS

$(e^x)' = e^x$, $(\ln x)' = \tfrac1x$, $(\sin x)' = \cos x$, $(\cos x)' = -\sin x$

$(a^x)' = \ln a \cdot a^x$

PRODUCT RULE

$(uv)' = u'v + uv'$, proved with the difference quotient.

$(x^2 e^x)' = (x^2 + 2x)e^x$

CHAIN RULE

$\left(u(v(x))\right)' = u'(v(x)) \cdot v'(x)$

$\left(\ln(3x - 5)\right)' = \tfrac{3}{3x - 5}$

REVERSAL

Antiderivative $F' = f$; for $x^n$: $\tfrac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C$ ($n \neq -1$).

$F' = 3x^2 + 4x$, $F(1) = 5$: $F = x^3 + 2x^2 + 2$
